album: For the Sake of the Song
label: Poppy
description: Townes Van Zandt's debut was cut in Houston and then buried under strings and horns he never asked for and spent the rest of his life disowning, but 'Waiting Around to Die' and the title track already show the flat, unhurried baritone and plainspoken dread that define him. It is rougher and more ornamented than what followed, a folk singer still being pushed toward a Nashville pop sound. Even so, it is the first document of the Houston coffeehouse scene that runs through the whole Texas songwriter lineage.
lineage: Grew out of the Houston folk clubs (the Jester Lounge, Sand Mountain) around Guy Clark and Mickey Newbury, and opened the account that Guy Clark, Steve Earle and, later, Jason Molina and Big Thief would keep drawing on.
key_tracks: For the Sake of the Song

label: Poppy
description: Recorded in Nashville with a full studio band behind him, this second album is Townes at his most narrative and gothic, from the drowned-sailor ache of 'Tecumseh Valley' to the astral drift of the title track. His voice is drier and more direct than on the debut, with strings and brushed drums kept low so the words carry the weight. 'Kathleen' and 'St. John the Gambler' show the doom-laced, half-mystical imagery that would mark his writing for the rest of his career.
lineage: A direct continuation of the Houston/Nashville songwriter circuit around Guy Clark and Mickey Newbury; its bleak, riverine imagery echoes forward into Steve Earle and Jason Molina's own flood-and-mountain songs.

label: Poppy
description: The self-titled third album is where most listeners now start: 'Lungs,' 'Nothin'' and '(Quicksilver Daydreams of) Maria' strip the arrangements down to guitar, light strings and his flat, exhausted voice. It is the record where his songwriting fully separates from the coffeehouse-folk pack, closer to existentialist dread than Woody Guthrie protest. Producer Jack Clement's spare, unhurried sessions let a song like 'None but the Rain' sit in silence instead of building toward a chorus.
lineage: The foundational record of the Texas songwriter tradition this lane is named for, echoed directly in Guy Clark and Steve Earle and, generations later, in Jason Molina's and Big Thief's own hushed, plainspoken folk songwriting.

label: Poppy
description: Cut in New York rather than Nashville, Delta Momma Blues is looser and bluesier than the two records before it, opening with the tumbling 'FFV' and closing on the stark, string-laced 'Silver Ships of Andilar.' Jack Clement again keeps the arrangements out of the way, letting Townes's guitar and cracked-dry voice carry most of the record. 'Come Tomorrow' and 'Where I Lead Me' trade in wry, boozy character sketches rather than the outright bleakness of his earlier work.
lineage: Bridges the early Poppy Records run with the harder-touring, harder-drinking persona that Blaze Foley and the outlaw wing of the Texas scene would later pick up wholesale.

label: Poppy
description: Released the same year as Delta Momma Blues, this one opens on the gospel-tinged 'Two Hands' and includes 'To Live Is to Fly,' one of the most covered songs in the whole Texas songwriter canon. The backing band is fuller than on the debut but still leaves room around his voice, letting the melodies rather than the arrangements carry the songs. Where much of his catalog sits in pure bleakness, 'To Live Is to Fly' and 'Highway Kind' reach for a weary, resigned kind of warmth instead.
lineage: 'To Live Is to Fly' became a standard covered by Guy Clark, Cowboy Junkies and Gillian Welch, carrying the Poppy Records-era songwriting straight into the alt-country and indie-folk generations.

album: The Late Great Townes Van Zandt
label: Poppy
description: The last of his original Poppy Records run pairs devastating originals like 'Pancho and Lefty' and 'If I Needed You' with wry novelty pieces ('German Mustard (A Clapalong)') and a cover of the country standard 'Fraulein', showing the funny-sad range that made him a songwriter's songwriter rather than a commercial act. The production is a little brighter than his early records, but his rasp-edged baritone still sits dead center in the mix. 'Pancho and Lefty' would become a number-one country hit for Willie Nelson and Merle Haggard a decade later.
lineage: Contains the two songs ('Pancho and Lefty,' 'If I Needed You') most responsible for carrying Townes's name past the Texas songwriter circle into outlaw and mainstream country.

album: Live at the Old Quarter, Houston, Texas
label: Tomato
description: Recorded solo over two nights in July 1973 at Houston's Old Quarter club but not released until 1977 after Poppy Records had folded, this is generally considered the definitive Townes document: just his voice, his guitar and a small, attentive room. The between-song banter is as much a part of the record as the songs, and stripped of studio arrangements, 'Pancho and Lefty,' 'If I Needed You' and 'Waitin' Around to Die' land even harder. It is the record most often handed to someone hearing him for the first time.
lineage: The touchstone live-solo-singer-songwriter record for the whole Texas lane, a direct model for later stripped-down live documents by Guy Clark and Robert Earl Keen.

label: Tomato
description: His first studio record in six years, produced by Chips Moman in Nashville, Flyin' Shoes softens the arrangements with light electric guitar and rhythm section but keeps the songs just as unsparing, from the loping title track to 'No Place to Fall' and 'Rex's Blues.' It is a more resigned, worn-in record than his early-'70s run, the sound of a writer settling into an itinerant, hard-drinking life rather than fighting it. A cover of Bo Diddley's 'Who Do You Love?' is the one moment of outright rock and roll on the record.
lineage: Closes out the classic-era Townes catalog before the long gap to At My Window, and 'No Place to Fall' became another widely covered standard for the Texas songwriter tradition.

label: Sugar Hill
description: After a nine-year gap, At My Window found Townes on Sugar Hill Records with a rawer, more haggard voice but the same unflinching eye, from the title track's domestic dread to 'Snowin' on Raton' and a rewrite of 'Marie' about a homeless couple's stillbirth. The production is spare acoustic-and-pedal-steel, closer in spirit to the Old Quarter tapes than to the Nashville sessions of the 1970s. It is the record that reintroduced him to a college-radio and Americana audience just as the genre was forming around songwriters like him.
lineage: An essential later record that carried Townes's songwriting directly into the Sugar Hill/Americana world that Nanci Griffith, Lyle Lovett and Robert Earl Keen were also recording into.

label: RCA Victor
description: Guy Clark's debut is the founding document of Texas songwriter craft: 'L.A. Freeway,' 'Desperados Waiting for a Train' and 'She Ain't Goin' Nowhere' are built from plain, exact detail rather than metaphor, sung in his dry, unhurried Texas drawl over acoustic and dobro. Nashville sidemen (Hargus 'Pig' Robbins, Johnny Gimble) keep the arrangements warm and uncluttered, closer to a back-porch session than a Music Row record. It set the template that Steve Earle, Rodney Crowell and Lyle Lovett would all later credit directly.
lineage: Grew out of the same Houston folk scene as Townes Van Zandt and Mickey Newbury; its plainspoken, detail-driven songwriting is the direct model for Rodney Crowell, Steve Earle and the Nashville songwriter tradition that follows.

label: RCA Victor
description: Clark's second album keeps the same Nashville-session craftsmanship as Old No. 1 but loosens up, with the title track and 'The Ballad of Laverne and Captain Flint' bringing in more humor and narrative sprawl. His voice stays conversational rather than showy, letting lines like 'Anyhow, I Love You' land as spoken confession. It didn't sell, and RCA dropped him after it, but it deepened the same plain-spoken storytelling that made his debut a songwriter's touchstone.
lineage: A direct continuation of the Old No. 1 songwriting style, later covered and cited by Rodney Crowell and the wider Nashville songwriter circle Clark helped seed.
key_tracks: The Ballad of Laverne and Captain Flint

label: Warner Bros.
description: Dropped by RCA, Clark moved to Warner Bros. for this self-titled third album, opening with 'Fool on the Roof' and 'Fools for Each Other' and staying close to the same acoustic, dobro-and-fiddle sound as his first two records. 'Houston Kid' and 'Comfort and Crazy' show him writing more explicitly autobiographical material than before. It rounds out what is generally treated as his classic-era trilogy before a long gap in his recording career.
lineage: Closes the 1970s run of Guy Clark records that established the songwriting standard Texas and Nashville songwriters kept measuring themselves against for decades after.

label: Asylum
description: Two decades on from Old No. 1, Dublin Blues finds Clark's voice weathered but his songwriting as exact as ever, from the title track's mix of homesickness for Texas and a bar in Ireland to the closing 'The Randall Knife,' a spoken-sung elegy for his father's pocketknife that is one of the most direct songs he ever wrote. Co-writes with Rodney Crowell and Townes-adjacent picker Verlon Thompson keep the arrangements small: acoustic guitar, dobro, almost no drums. It is the record most often cited as his best later-career work.
lineage: An essential later record showing the Old No. 1 songwriting style fully matured, recorded alongside the 1990s Nashville Americana scene that Rodney Crowell and Steve Earle were also part of.

label: Sugar Hill
description: Cold Dog Soup pairs Clark with young Nashville writers (Shawn Camp, Verlon Thompson) and includes a spare cover of Steve Earle's 'Fort Worth Blues,' written for Townes Van Zandt after his death, alongside originals like 'Sis Draper' and 'Water Under the Bridge.' The record stays in the same acoustic-first, dobro-and-fiddle sound as Dublin Blues, unhurried and conversational. It is a late-career example of the songwriter's-songwriter role Clark had settled into by the 1990s, mentoring and co-writing as much as performing.
lineage: Part of the same 1990s Sugar Hill/Nashville songwriter circle as Dublin Blues, directly tying Clark's original 1970s Texas songwriting to the Americana format that formed around it.

label: Atco
description: Jerry Jeff Walker's debut is a folk-troubadour record built around the title song, written after he met an itinerant street performer in a New Orleans jail cell and covered by dozens of artists ever after. The rest of the album stays in a gentle, string-and-guitar folk-pop mode, closer to the Greenwich Village scene he had come out of than to the rowdy Texas records he would make a few years later. It is the last record before he relocated to Austin and became a central figure of the progressive country scene.
lineage: Predates Walker's move to Austin; 'Mr. Bojangles' itself became one of the most widely covered songs to come out of the Texas songwriter world, recorded by everyone from Nina Simone to the Nitty Gritty Dirt Band.

label: MCA
description: Recorded after Walker settled in Austin, this self-titled album is looser and more countrified than his New York folk records, mixing his own 'Gettin' By' and 'Gypsy Songman' with early covers of Guy Clark's 'L.A. Freeway' and Ray Wylie Hubbard-adjacent material. The band leans into pedal steel and honky-tonk piano rather than folk-pop strings, matching the loose, beer-hall feel of the Austin scene he had just joined. It is the transitional record between Walker the folk singer and Walker the ringleader of Austin's progressive-country crowd.
lineage: Marks Walker's turn from Greenwich Village folk toward the Austin cosmic-cowboy scene that would produce ¡Viva Terlingua! a year later, and helped introduce Guy Clark's songwriting to a wider audience.

label: MCA
description: Recorded live (with some studio overdubs) at a dance hall in Luckenbach with his backing group the Lost Gonzo Band, ¡Viva Terlingua! is the record most often pointed to as the sound of Austin's early-1970s progressive-country scene: rowdy, funny, unpolished, and full of songs by Walker's friends rather than just his own. It introduced Ray Wylie Hubbard's 'Up Against the Wall, Redneck Mother' and Guy Clark's 'Desperados Waiting for a Train' to a wide audience, and Gary P. Nunn's 'London Homesick Blues' became a de facto Austin anthem. The loose, beer-drenched performance energy is as important to the record as any single song.
lineage: The clearest document of the cosmic-cowboy/progressive-country scene that Michael Martin Murphey and Willie Nelson's move to Austin also fed, and a direct influence on the outlaw-country movement's live, unpolished aesthetic.
key_tracks: Up Against the Wall, Redneck Mother

album: More a Legend Than a Band
label: Rounder
description: Recorded in a single week in Nashville in 1972 by Jimmie Dale Gilmore, Joe Ely and Butch Hancock as an acoustic string band with musical saw and dobro, these sessions were barely released at the time (briefly, only on 3.8mm eight-track tape) and only reached listeners properly in 1990 as this compilation. Songs like 'Dallas,' 'Jole Blon' and 'Tonight I Think I'm Gonna Go Downtown' mix plainspoken West Texas storytelling with a spacey, almost mystical folk sound unlike anything else in the scene. It became one of the most influential 'lost' records in Americana, cited constantly once it finally circulated.
lineage: The founding document of the Lubbock songwriter triangle, sending Gilmore, Ely and Hancock off on separate solo careers that all fed back into the same scene; its legend-before-band reputation directly shaped how Uncle Tupelo-era alt-country writers talked about authenticity.
borderline_note: Recorded in 1972 but not meaningfully released until this 1990 Rounder compilation of those sessions; logged under its actual first wide release year rather than the obscure 1972 eight-track pressing.

label: MCA
description: Joe Ely's solo debut, cut with his hard-touring bar band (Lloyd Maines on pedal steel, Jesse Taylor on lead guitar), turns Butch Hancock's 'She Never Spoke Spanish to Me' and his own 'Gambler's Bride' into full-band, rock-tempo country rather than the acoustic sound of the Flatlanders sessions he'd just come out of. His voice is a rough, urgent yelp rather than a crooner's, closer to a bar-band frontman than a folk singer. It set him apart immediately from the other two Flatlanders as the rocking, road-dog wing of the Lubbock songwriter triangle.
lineage: Grew directly out of the Flatlanders' breakup and Butch Hancock's songwriting; its full-band, rock-forward take on West Texas songwriting is a direct antecedent of the alt-country bands that followed a decade later.
key_tracks: She Never Spoke Spanish to Me
I Had My Hopes Up High

label: MCA
description: Ely's second album leans harder into the road-band sound, built almost entirely from Butch Hancock songs ('Boxcars,' 'West Texas Waltz,' the title track) plus a cover of his own Flatlanders-era 'Tonight I Think I'm Gonna Go Downtown'-style material and a rocked-up 'Honky Tonkin'.' Jesse Taylor's lead guitar and Lloyd Maines's pedal steel trade off constantly, giving the record a rowdier, more electric feel than most Texas songwriter records of the era. It is generally considered his defining 1970s album.
lineage: Cemented Butch Hancock as a songwriter working through Ely's rocking band arrangements, a combination that fed directly into the Uncle Tupelo/alt-country generation's own hard-driving take on country songwriting.

label: MCA
description: The third Ely/Hancock collaboration is darker and less immediate than Honky Tonk Masquerade, with the title track (named for Austin's Guadalupe Street strip) and 'Fools Fall in Love' leaning into dense, moody band interplay rather than barroom rave-ups. Saxophonist Bobby Keys-adjacent horn player Ed Vizard's 'BBQ and Foam' adds a rougher, almost punk-inflected edge that points toward the Clash tour Ely would join the following year. Ely and Lloyd Maines were reportedly unhappy with the production at the time, but it has aged into a respected, slightly overlooked entry in the run.
lineage: Its harder, less polished sound anticipates the punk-adjacent audience Ely found when the Clash invited his band on tour, a rare direct bridge between Texas progressive country and UK punk.

label: MCA
description: Recorded in London on the tour where the Clash brought Ely's band out as an opening act, Live Shots catches the Joe Ely Band at full, sweat-through-the-shirt intensity, tearing through 'Fingernails,' 'Honky Tonk Masquerade' and 'Honky Tonkin'' at a harder, faster clip than the studio versions. The set draws almost entirely from the first three albums, functioning as a document of just how far Ely's band had pushed West Texas songwriting toward rock and roll. It became a touchstone for the punk-adjacent audience that first connected with Ely through the Clash.
lineage: A direct product of the Clash/Joe Ely Band connection, one of the clearest real-world links between Texas progressive country and the UK punk scene of the same moment.

album: West Texas Waltzes & Dust-Blown Tractor Tunes
label: Rainlight
description: Butch Hancock's solo debut, self-released on his own Rainlight label after the Flatlanders broke up, is stark acoustic guitar and voice with almost no studio polish, songs like 'West Texas Waltz' and 'You've Never Seen Me Cry' built from flat, wide-open prairie imagery. It is the most purely folk of the three Lubbock songwriters' records, closer to Townes Van Zandt's bare arrangements than to Joe Ely's full-band rock. Hancock would go on to write many of the songs Ely and Jimmie Dale Gilmore made famous under their own names.
lineage: Established Hancock as the songwriter engine of the Lubbock triangle, supplying material that Joe Ely turned into full-band rock and Jimmie Dale Gilmore turned into honky-tonk covers throughout the 1980s.

label: Rainlight
description: Hancock's second Rainlight self-release stays in the same spare, home-label mode as his debut, with the title track and 'Neon Wind' extending the plainspoken West Texas character studies he had already established. The recordings are unglamorous and a little rough at the edges, made on his own terms and outside any Nashville or Austin studio system. It remains one of the harder-to-find records in the Lubbock triangle's catalog, prized by collectors of the scene.
lineage: Continues the self-released, DIY model Hancock kept using throughout his career, a direct precedent for the independent-label ethos later Texas and alt-country songwriters relied on.

label: HighTone
description: After more than a decade away from recording, Jimmie Dale Gilmore's solo debut leans into classic honky-tonk phrasing, opening with a cover of his own Flatlanders-era 'White Freight Liner Blues' and Butch Hancock's 'Honky Tonk Masquerade' alongside originals like the title track. His high, keening tenor, closer to Hank Williams than to Townes Van Zandt's flat baritone, gives even Hancock's darkest songs an almost gospel lift. It reintroduced Gilmore as a solo artist just as the Flatlanders' reputation was starting to grow.
lineage: An essential later record from the Lubbock triangle, turning Butch Hancock's songwriting into classic honky-tonk vocal performance and helping set up the trio's eventual reunion.

label: HighTone
description: Gilmore's second HighTone album keeps the same honky-tonk core band but draws more from his own writing and from Hancock's catalog, mixing traditional-leaning arrangements with the spacey, almost meditative quality his voice brings to any song. It shows the influence of his years studying with a meditation teacher in Colorado as much as his years fronting the Flatlanders, giving even simple country structures an unusually calm, floating quality. It further built the reputation that led to his 1991 Elektra deal.
lineage: Deepens the honky-tonk-by-way-of-Lubbock sound Gilmore established on Fair & Square, bridging the Flatlanders' 1972 sessions and his eventual mainstream Nashville-adjacent career.
key_tracks: Just a Wave, Not the Water
Treat Me Like a Saturday Night

label: Outhouse Records
description: Recorded during Blaze Foley's final run of shows at a small Austin club in 1988, just months before he was shot and killed, this tape (first circulated on cassette in 1989) is the fullest surviving document of his voice: a rumbling baritone, self-deprecating stage patter, and songs like 'Clay Pigeons' and 'If I Could Only Fly' that move between wrecked tenderness and dark comedy in a single verse. The recording is rough and close-mic'd, a bar tape rather than a studio session, which only adds to its legend. It is the record most responsible for Foley's posthumous reputation as, in Lucinda Williams's and Townes Van Zandt's shared estimation, one of the best songwriters to come out of the Austin scene.
lineage: Documents the Austin outlaw-folk fringe around Townes Van Zandt that Foley belonged to; 'If I Could Only Fly' and 'Clay Pigeons' went on to be covered by Merle Haggard, Lucinda Williams and John Prine, carrying his songwriting far past the small club it was taped in.
borderline_note: First circulated as a 1989 cassette on the tiny Outhouse label; later CD/vinyl reissues on Lost Art Records are the same performance, not a separate release, so it is logged under its original 1989 year.

label: Fat Possum
description: Compiled from home and studio sessions Foley cut in 1976 with his early duo partner Gordon Fowler, long before the Austin Outhouse tapes, The Dawg Years is looser and stranger than the later live record, mixing sincere songs like 'Livin' in the Woods in a Tree' with joke numbers ('Cosmic Doo Doo,' 'Big Cheeseburgers and Good French Fries'). The fidelity is rough four-track cassette, closer to a scrapbook than a finished album, but it fills in Foley's formative years before he became the Austin scene's most famous almost-star. Fat Possum's archival release finally gave these tapes a proper, legitimate release decades after his death.
lineage: An archival release of pre-fame recordings by the same Austin outlaw-folk songwriter documented on Live at the Austin Outhouse, filling out the picture of Foley's writing before Townes Van Zandt and the Outhouse crowd took notice of him.
key_tracks: Livin' in the Woods in a Tree

label: Smash
borderline_note: Blends British Invasion pop, Tex-Mex conjunto and blue-eyed soul as much as country; included for the country-flecked 'Texas Me' and Doug Sahm's role as a hub figure the rest of the Austin/San Antonio scene grew around.
description: Doug Sahm's band scored a fluke hit with the title track's organ-driven pop-soul, but Mendocino also holds 'Texas Me,' a homesick country song that shows the Texas roots underneath the British Invasion surface. Sahm's band moves between garage rock, Cajun-tinged Tex-Mex and country phrasing within a single side, a restlessness that became his signature. Recorded in San Francisco during his brief psychedelic-era relocation, it still sounds unmistakably like a Texas band abroad.
lineage: Doug Sahm became a connective figure for the whole Texas scene, recording later with Bob Dylan, Willie Nelson and Flaco Jiménez and directly inspiring the genre-blending, Tex-Mex-inflected side of Texas progressive country.

label: Atlantic
description: Recorded in New York with Bob Dylan, Dr. John and David Bromberg sitting in, Doug Sahm and Band moves freely between honky-tonk ('(Is Anybody Going to) San Antone'), Bob Wills-style Western swing ('Faded Love') and horn-driven Texas soul, a genre-hopping range few of his peers could match. Sahm's rough, conversational voice holds the whole thing together, treating country, blues and conjunto as one continuous Texas sound rather than separate styles. It sold poorly at the time but is now regarded as one of the era's great Texas roots records.
lineage: A hub record for the whole scene, pulling in Bob Dylan as a collaborator and folding conjunto, Western swing and honky-tonk into a single album the way the Austin and San Antonio scenes were doing on stage.

label: Atlantic
description: Assembled from leftover material from the same October 1972 Atlantic sessions as Doug Sahm and Band, Texas Tornado leans harder into country and blues, with the title track and 'Blue Horizon' built around pedal steel and Sahm's talk-singing delivery. 'Chicano' and 'Juan Mendoza' bring in the conjunto and Tex-Mex side of his San Antonio upbringing more directly than the first album did. It confirmed Sahm as a bandleader who treated the whole spectrum of Texas roots music as a single repertoire.
lineage: Companion record to Doug Sahm and Band, further cementing the Tex-Mex/country/soul fusion that made Sahm a bridge figure between the Austin scene and San Antonio's conjunto tradition.

label: Shelter
description: The only album Willis Alan Ramsey ever released, produced by Leon Russell's Shelter Records, is a warm, unhurried collection of character songs, most famously 'Muskrat Candlelight' (a hit for America and later the Captain & Tennille as 'Muskrat Love') and the much-covered 'Ballad of Spider John.' His finger-picked guitar and easy, conversational voice sit closer to a campfire singer than a studio pro, and the whole record has a loose, funny warmth rare in the more bleak Texas songwriter catalog. Its cult reputation has only grown with the decades of silence that followed it.
lineage: A key Austin-scene contemporary of Jerry Jeff Walker and Guy Clark; 'Ballad of Spider John' and 'Muskrat Candlelight' were widely covered and helped establish the Austin songwriter circle's reputation in Nashville and beyond.

label: A&M
description: Michael Martin Murphey's debut, produced by Bob Johnston in Nashville, mixes protest songwriting (the title track's sympathy for Geronimo) with the loose, string-band feel that became known as 'cosmic cowboy' music back in Austin. 'Backslider's Wine' would later become a Viva Terlingua highlight in Jerry Jeff Walker's hands, showing how tightly the Austin songwriters traded material. Rolling Stone singled him out early as one of the best new songwriters in the country, and the record helped put Austin's emerging scene on the national map.
lineage: Coined and popularized the 'cosmic cowboy' tag for the Austin progressive-country scene, directly feeding the same circle that produced Jerry Jeff Walker's Viva Terlingua and B.W. Stevenson's records.

label: A&M
description: Murphey's second album names the Austin scene outright with 'Cosmic Cowboy, Pt. 1' and 'Alleys of Austin,' turning the loose, country-rock-meets-folk sound of his debut into a genre statement. The songs stretch out more than typical AM radio country, with 'South Canadian River Song' running past seven minutes on gentle, unhurried instrumental passages. It is the record most responsible for putting a name on the whole hippie-country movement gathering around the Armadillo World Headquarters in Austin.
lineage: Gave the 'cosmic cowboy' scene its name, directly describing the same Austin crowd (Jerry Jeff Walker, Willie Nelson, Rusty Wier) that the rest of this lane's Austin artists belonged to.

label: RCA Victor
borderline_note: Leans further toward pop-country crossover than most of this lane thanks to the 'My Maria' hit single, but Stevenson came directly out of the Austin cosmic-cowboy circle alongside Murphey and Fromholz.
description: B.W. Stevenson's biggest album pairs two hit singles, the string-swept 'My Maria' (a Billboard top-ten hit, later a country number one for Brooks & Dunn) and 'Shambala' (also a hit the same year for Three Dog Night), with rootsier, band-driven material like 'Sunset Woman.' His big, husky voice pushes the record toward pop-country crossover more than most of this lane, but he came directly out of the same Austin cosmic-cowboy circle as Michael Martin Murphey. It is the commercial high point of the whole progressive-country movement's brief brush with the pop charts.
lineage: Part of the Austin cosmic-cowboy circle around Murphey and Steve Fromholz; its crossover success showed Nashville and the pop charts that Austin's songwriters could compete commercially, briefly.

album: Don't It Make You Wanna Dance?
label: 20th Century Records
description: Rusty Wier's best-known album is built for a Saturday-night dancehall crowd, the title track (later a bigger hit for Bonnie Raitt-adjacent bar bands and a country radio staple) driven by a hard-strummed electric guitar and Wier's raspy, good-time shout. It stays close to the honky-tonk-meets-rock energy of the Armadillo World Headquarters crowd rather than the more introspective songwriting of Townes Van Zandt or Guy Clark. Wier was a fixture of the Austin scene's rowdier, bar-band side throughout the 1970s.
lineage: Represents the dancehall, bar-band end of the Austin cosmic-cowboy scene alongside Jerry Jeff Walker's Lost Gonzo Band and Michael Martin Murphey's early records.
key_tracks: Don't It Make You Wanna Dance?

label: Landfall
description: A visual artist as much as a musician, Terry Allen's debut is a self-contained concept record, a stark murder-and-flight narrative following two couples from Southern California to the Texas-Mexico border, sung over sparse piano and rough acoustic guitar. It plays more like a song cycle or a spoken-word art piece than a conventional singer-songwriter album, closer to Randy Newman's character studies than to Guy Clark's plainspoken narratives. Self-released in a small pressing, it became a cult object among the Lubbock and Austin scenes before slowly gaining wider recognition.
lineage: Allen came out of the same Lubbock art-and-music circle as the Flatlanders and Terry Allen's own visual-art career; Juarez's conceptual, gothic storytelling is a direct forerunner of the Southern-gothic strain later heard in Drive-By Truckers and Jason Molina.

label: Fate
description: A sprawling double album cut with a crack Lubbock studio band (Lloyd Maines, Ponty Bone, Jesse Taylor), Lubbock (on everything) turns Allen's flat, talk-singing baritone loose on satirical, affectionate portraits of his hometown, from the honky-tonk stomp of 'Amarillo Highway' to the surreal 'The Wolfman of Del Rio.' It is funnier and looser than Juarez, closer to a barroom song cycle than an art piece, though the same eye for grotesque, specific detail runs through both records. It has become one of the most cited 'lost classics' of the whole Texas songwriter scene.
lineage: Shares its core Lubbock studio band with Joe Ely's late-'70s records, and its satirical small-town storytelling is a direct ancestor of Drive-By Truckers' and Todd Snider's own funny-bleak Southern narratives.

album: A Rumor in My Own Time
label: Capitol
description: Steve Fromholz's Capitol Records debut is a warm, wry singer-songwriter record, mixing plainspoken character songs ('Hobo Bob') with the loose humor ('Ain't It Nice to Be Alone') that made him one of the Austin scene's most beloved live performers. His songwriting, including the much-covered 'Texas Trilogy' suite (first recorded on his earlier Frummox album), balances comic timing with real tenderness for small-town Texas life. He would go on to be named Texas poet laureate, and this record is generally considered his strongest studio statement.
lineage: A central Austin-scene songwriter alongside Guy Clark and Jerry Jeff Walker; 'Texas Trilogy' has been covered by Lyle Lovett and remains one of the most enduring pieces of writing to come out of the progressive-country movement.
key_tracks: Ain't It Nice to Be Alone

label: Vanguard
description: Fronting his band the Texas Jewboys, Kinky Friedman's debut is satirical outlaw country, using broad comedy ('Get Your Biscuits in the Oven and Your Buns in the Bed') and pointed political songwriting ('Ride 'Em Jewboy,' about the Holocaust; 'The Ballad of Charles Whitman,' about the UT Tower shooting) in the same set. His deadpan half-spoken drawl and the band's straight honky-tonk backing let the jokes and the genuinely dark material sit side by side without either undercutting the other. It made him a cult figure on the outlaw-country circuit well before his later career as a novelist and politician.
lineage: A satirical, provocation-first extension of the outlaw-country scene around Willie Nelson and Waylon Jennings; its funny-sad, taboo-baiting songwriting anticipates the deadpan school that runs from John Prine through Drag City decades later.

label: ABC Records
description: Friedman's second album keeps the Texas Jewboys' straight honky-tonk backing and adds guest turns from Eric Clapton and Bob Dylan's touring band, giving songs like 'Wild Man from Borneo' a bigger, more polished sound than the scrappier Sold American. The satire stays sharp, but there is more straight character songwriting mixed in alongside the provocations. It kept Friedman in the outlaw-country conversation even as his novelty reputation started to overshadow his actual songwriting.
lineage: A continuation of the Sold American persona within the outlaw-country mainstream, recorded with musicians from Bob Dylan's own circle.
key_tracks: Somebody's Been Sleeping in My Bed

album: Ray Wylie Hubbard and the Cowboy Twinkies
label: Reprise
description: Ray Wylie Hubbard's debut with his full electric band the Cowboy Twinkies mixes rough honky-tonk rockers ('$60 Ford,' 'West Texas Country Western Dance Band') with looser, funkier material, a rowdier and more band-driven record than his songwriting reputation might suggest. It came out two years after Jerry Jeff Walker's live cover of his 'Up Against the Wall, Redneck Mother' had already made Hubbard's name known across the outlaw-country scene, though that song itself wouldn't appear on one of his own studio records for a few more years. Reprise dropped the band after this one record, and Hubbard spent much of the following decade fighting addiction before his celebrated comeback.
lineage: Hubbard's songwriting (especially the still-unrecorded-by-him 'Redneck Mother') was already central to the outlaw-country scene via Jerry Jeff Walker's cover, tying this record directly to the ¡Viva Terlingua! circle.
key_tracks: West Texas Country Western Dance Band

label: Lone Star Records
description: Off the Wall finally gives Hubbard his own studio recording of 'Redneck Mother,' the song Jerry Jeff Walker had made a scene anthem five years earlier, alongside rowdy new material like 'Mexico Bar' and the loping 'Prairie Madness.' The band is leaner and twangier than the Cowboy Twinkies' sound, closer to straight honky-tonk with a rock rhythm section. It is a transitional record between Hubbard's hard-partying 1970s persona and the more spiritually searching, fingerpicked songwriter he would become decades later.
lineage: Reclaims 'Redneck Mother' for its own writer after Jerry Jeff Walker's Viva Terlingua made it an outlaw-country standard, closing the loop on one of the scene's most-covered songs.

album: There's a Light Beyond These Woods
label: B.F. Deal Records
description: Nanci Griffith's self-released debut, cut for a tiny Austin label while she was still working as a kindergarten teacher, is spare acoustic-folk songwriting sung in her light, girlish voice, closer to the John Denver/Judy Collins folk tradition than to the rowdier progressive-country records around her. Song titles about small-town Texas life and quiet coming-of-age moments set the template for everything she recorded afterward. It sold only regionally at the time but is now treated as the first chapter of one of the era's most acclaimed folk-country careers.
lineage: The starting point of Griffith's career inside the Austin folk scene that also nurtured Lyle Lovett and Robert Earl Keen; her plainspoken, small-town storytelling runs in a direct line from Guy Clark's example.
key_tracks: There's a Light Beyond These Woods

album: Once in a Very Blue Moon
label: Philo
description: Recorded in Nashville with producer Jim Rooney and a first-call bluegrass band (Béla Fleck, Mark O'Connor), Once in a Very Blue Moon is where Griffith's clear, delicate voice first meets real studio polish without losing the plainspoken folk core of her early records. 'Love at the Five and Dime,' her own song about small-town romance, would soon become a bigger hit in Kathy Mattea's hands, showing how directly her Texas folk songwriting was starting to feed the Nashville mainstream. The record marks the turn from regional folk singer to a figure the wider Americana and country world was starting to notice.
lineage: Bridges Griffith's Austin folk beginnings with the Nashville session-musician world, the same crossover path Guy Clark and Rodney Crowell had already opened up for Texas songwriters.
key_tracks: Love at the Five and Dime
Once in a Very Blue Moon

album: The Last of the True Believers
label: Philo
description: The last of Griffith's Philo Records run, The Last of the True Believers pairs 'Love at the Five and Dime' (here in its original recorded home) with 'Lone Star State of Mind' and further first-call Nashville session players, pushing her sound closer to the acoustic Americana mainstream that would soon embrace her fully. Her voice stays light and conversational even as the arrangements grow fuller, keeping the small-town Texas detail of her earlier records intact. It was her last independent-label album before she signed to MCA and became a national name.
lineage: Caps Griffith's Austin-to-Nashville arc that began with There's a Light Beyond These Woods, and directly set up her major-label career alongside fellow Texas songwriters Lyle Lovett and Robert Earl Keen.
key_tracks: Love at the Five and Dime

label: Workshop Records
description: Robert Earl Keen's debut, cut for a tiny Austin label with a young Lyle Lovett co-writing 'The Front Porch Song' and Nanci Griffith singing harmony, is plainspoken acoustic songwriting directly descended from Guy Clark and Townes Van Zandt's example. Keen's dry Texas drawl and narrative instinct are already fully formed here, on story-songs like 'Swervin' in My Lane' and the title track. It is a low-budget, low-key record that only found its wider audience once Keen and Lovett had both become better known.
lineage: Documents the mid-1980s Texas A&M/Austin songwriter circle that produced both Keen and Lyle Lovett, a direct continuation of the Guy Clark/Townes Van Zandt storytelling tradition into the next generation.

label: Sugar Hill
borderline_note: Recorded in 1989, at the edge of this lane's chronology and just before the Americana/alt-country format existed; included as an essential later record by a songwriter who started squarely inside this scene.
description: West Textures is the record that made Keen's name, built around 'The Road Goes On Forever,' a bank-robbery narrative that became one of the most covered songs in Texas songwriting and, decades later, a Joe Ely/Robert Earl Keen concert staple in its own right. The full-band arrangements (fiddle, pedal steel, a rock rhythm section) are fuller than his debut but still built to serve the story, never the hook. It is widely treated as a founding record of the alt-country and Texas-country movements that followed in the 1990s.
lineage: Keen's storytelling grew directly out of Guy Clark and Townes Van Zandt's example, and 'The Road Goes On Forever' in turn became a foundational text for the Texas/Red Dirt country scene of the 1990s and 2000s.
